quote: Your mandatory belief is that the egg’s probability of spontaneous reformation is ~0. Probabilities are not certainties, but the laws of probability are theorems.
content: The laws of probability are theorems; that a particular probability is “mandatory” is not, and the essay’s example is one where the gap is famous. The near-zero probability of the egg reassembling follows from the probability axioms only once one has a distribution over microstates, and the distribution used, uniform on the accessible phase space, is the fundamental postulate of statistical mechanics: a postulate, whose justification (ergodicity, typicality, maximum entropy) is the open problem of the field’s foundations (Uffink (2007)). The lottery believer’s error is real, and the essay is right that a probabilistic belief is not optional. But the rhetorical force of “mandatory” and “harder than steel” comes from calling a physical postulate a logical necessity, which is precisely the move the essay accuses its opponents of making in the other direction. A probability assignment is mandatory given a prior; the prior is a premise; and the essay’s theorem-talk conceals the premise in the one example chosen to make it look like there is none.

quote: Each extra detail in your argument necessarily decreases the joint proba­bility.
content: This confuses the probability of an argument’s premises with the probability of its conclusion. Adding a conjunct to a set of claims lowers the probability that all of them are true; that is the conjunction rule. But an argument is not a conjunction of its steps, and the probability of a conclusion is not the joint probability of everything said on the way to it. Two independent lines of evidence for a claim are “extra details” that raise its probability; a longer argument that supplies more evidence yields a higher posterior, not a lower one; and a step that is a disjunction of routes (“either A or B gets you there”) becomes more probable, not less, as routes are added. The rule the essay states is correct for a single conjunctive chain in which every link must hold, which is the structure of a perpetual-motion machine and of the “vast edifices” the essay has in mind. Stated as a law about arguments in general, “another gear makes your machine less efficient” would condemn every cumulative case in science and law, where the gears are the evidence. The conjunction fallacy (Tversky & Kahneman (1983)) is a bias about conjunctions; the essay has generalized it to a bias about length.

quote: And similarly, when half-trained or tenth-trained rationalists abandon their art and try to believe without evidence just this once, they often build vast edifices of justification, confusing themselves just enough to conceal the magical steps.
content: The psychological model here is that the elaborate argument is the mechanism by which the belief is produced, so that locating the magical step will dissolve the belief. The literature on motivated reasoning says the order is the reverse. Beliefs of this kind arrive first, by affect and social identification, and the argument is constructed afterward to justify them (Haidt (2001); Mercier & Sperber, whose argumentative theory Book I and II’s annotations discussed); when the argument is refuted the believer produces another, because the argument was never load-bearing. The essay’s own description supports this: the structure “tends to morph and squirm away as you interrogate them,” which is what one expects if the belief is causally upstream of the edifice. So “nailing down where the magic occurs” is a diagnosis of the wrong organ. The reactionless-drive inventor with the Excel spreadsheet is a good example of exactly this: he could not show the spreadsheet because the spreadsheet was not what convinced him.

quote: In classical mechanics, violating Conservation of Momentum is provably impossible. So any Excel spreadsheet calculated according to the rules of classical mechanics must necessarily show that no reactionless thrust exists—unless your machine is complicated enough that you have made a mistake in the calculations.
content: This is correct, and the subsequent history is a useful check on how the correction actually happens. In 2016 a NASA laboratory published, in a peer-reviewed propulsion journal, a measured thrust from a closed microwave cavity (White et al. (2017)), the “EmDrive,” a reactionless drive in exactly the essay’s sense. The claim was not disposed of by pointing to the theorem; it was disposed of by the Dresden group building a more sensitive balance and showing that the thrust was thermal expansion of the mounting and interaction with the Earth’s magnetic field (Tajmar, Neunzig and Weikert, “High-Accuracy Thrust Measurements of the EmDrive and Elimination of False-Positive Effects,” 2021). Everyone involved knew momentum was conserved; the theorem told them a mistake existed, and the experiment told them where. That is the practical content of the essay’s point, and it is weaker than the essay’s rhetoric: a conservation law licenses the belief that an error exists, not the belief that one need not look. The essay’s last line, “until he finally collected enough complications to make a mistake in his Excel spreadsheet,” gets it right; the demand at the start of the previous essay, “tell me which specific step violates the laws of physics,” is the one nobody in the EmDrive affair could satisfy until the measurement was done.
